To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the photo-z requirements for self-calibration are weaker than for non-self-calibrated analyses; and (2) the self-calibration of the dark energy equation-of-state parameter can be done with a training set that is smaller than the training set needed for self-calibration of both the dark energy and mass parameters simultaneously.

photo-z's with a bias and scatter of 0.003, and 0.02, respectively, are required for a 100 deg2 cluster survey with a yield of 500 clusters per square degree in order not to significantly degrade dark energy constraining power relative to the baseline cosmology.

1) photo-z requirements for cluster counts are comparable to those for weak lensing surveys; 2) the self-calibration of cluster surveys with photo-z's is feasible, though it is important to include external mass inferences; and 3) photo-z requirements are weaker than the baseline dark energy constrains for cluster surveys with a lower cluster yield and for smaller surveys.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the requirements on cluster photo-z's for future surveys, and the role of self-calibration in constraining dark energy.
the ability of galaxy clusters to constrain the dark energy.
the impact of cluster redshift uncertainties on dark energy constraints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
photo-z requirements are not stringent enough to be a major obstacle for cluster cosmology.
photo-z's need to be measured with a precision of ∼0.03 and an accuracy of ∼0 003.
cluster surveys need photo-z's with a precision and accuracy of 1%-2% and 0.5%, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cluster cosmology is very sensitive to photo-z errors, and that self-calibration is very useful in this context.

cluster surveys with photo-z requirements better than 0-0.01 and 0-0-03 are needed to constrain the dark energy equation-of-state parameters to 0.1 and 0.2, respectively, in the absence of external mass calibration.
photo-z requirements for cluster surveys are comparable to or even weaker than those required for weak lensing or baryon acoustic oscillation studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the requirements for the photo-z bias and scatter are not particularly stringent and that self-calibration can provide a valuable tool in the analysis of upcoming cluster surveys.
photo-z requirements for cluster cosmology are not prohibitive and can be met by ongoing and future surveys.
future cluster surveys will require accurate and precise photo-z estimates in order to achieve the desired constraining power.
